question: The largest whole number such that seven times the number is less than \(100\) is
solution:
We need the last whole number whose multiple of 7 is below 100. Since
\[
7\cdot14=98<100,
\qquad 7\cdot15=105>100,
\]
14 works and 15 does not. Every larger whole number has an even larger multiple of 7. Thus the largest possible number is \(\boxed{14}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

edges.reason: The general modeling routine transfers, but at-least/at-most relations and admissible integer solutions can be taught directly in inequalities; the equality-modeling family is preparation.
The modeled one-variable inequality must be solved before feasible quantities can be interpreted.

Written addition prepares vertical alignment and repeated carrying. In multiplication the carried amount is added to one digit product, so the full three-digit column-addition procedure is not executed.

The general digit-by-digit multiplication algorithm contains digit products with seven, eight and nine. Their values are required, without demanding rote recitation as the exclusive way to obtain them.
